sections.title: Continuity: the three-condition test & related topics

board_events.text: When is a function CONTINUOUS at a point?
Intuition: draw the graph through the point without lifting your pen — no jumps, no holes.
Condition 1: $f(c)$ exists — the function has a definite value at the point.
Condition 2: $\lim_{x\to c} f(x)$ exists — left and right approaches agree.
Condition 3: the limit equals the value — where it heads is where it lands.
All three must hold and agree. Break any one and $f$ is discontinuous.
Differentiability = smoothness, a stronger demand
Smooth road: one well-defined direction at every instant.
Sharp hairpin: no single direction at the kink — not differentiable.

segments.text: <curious>So when do we call a function continuous at a point? Let's build the idea from the ground up, then make it exam-precise.
Picture riding a train where the rails are joined end to end with no gap. The journey glides through. That unbroken path is continuity — you draw the graph through the point without lifting your pen.
But an examiner won't accept don't lift your pen, so we pin it down with three conditions. First, the function must actually exist at the point — f of c has a definite value.
Second, the function must head somewhere definite as you approach. The limit as x tends to c must exist, which needs the approach from the left and from the right to agree.
Written out, the left-hand limit must equal the right-hand limit. If the two sides aim for different heights, you get a jump and the limit simply fails to exist.
Third, the subtle one: where the function is heading must match where it actually lands. The limit has to equal f of c itself.
So the limit as x tends to c equals f of c — one clean equation that quietly packages all three demands into a single test you can apply.
If even one of these fails, the function snaps. A jump when the two sides disagree, a removable hole when they agree but the dot sits somewhere else.
Continuity only asks that the graph be unbroken. Differentiability asks for something stronger — that the graph be smooth, with no sharp corners anywhere.
Think of a long, gently banked expressway curve. You keep the wheel turning smoothly, and at every instant there is exactly one direction you are pointing. That is a differentiable path.

Now a sharp hairpin in the Ghats that suddenly kinks. At the corner there is no single direction — you point one way an instant before and another way after. That corner is non-differentiable, even though the road never broke.

The classic mathematical hairpin is the absolute value function at zero. The graph is a perfect V: unbroken, but at the tip the slope is minus one coming in and plus one going out. No single tangent, so continuous but not differentiable.
This gives us the most important sentence in the whole subtopic, and examiners test it relentlessly, so lock it in now.
<whisper>Differentiability is strictly stronger than continuity. Every differentiable function is continuous — smooth implies unbroken.
The reverse is false. A continuous function need not be differentiable — the V is unbroken yet cornered. Memorise the direction of that arrow; it only runs one way.

Smoothness can fail three ways: a corner like the V, a cusp or vertical tangent like the cube root at zero where the slope blows up, and anywhere the function is already broken — a break kills smoothness automatically.
Let's collect the exact machinery you actually compute with. Everything reduces to left-hand and right-hand quantities built with a small positive step h.
Continuity at c in one line: the limit equals the value, which unpacks to left-hand limit equals right-hand limit equals f of c. All three tied together.
Writing h tending to zero from the positive side, the left-hand limit uses c minus h, and the right-hand limit uses c plus h. Same little h, approached from the two sides.
Differentiability at c means this single limit — the difference quotient — exists and is finite. That is the instantaneous slope, the derivative at the point.
It splits into one-sided derivatives. The left-hand derivative uses the left piece, with the step being minus h in the denominator because you moved backward.
The right-hand derivative uses the right piece with an ordinary plus h step. Differentiable at c means these two are equal and both finite.
And the bridge theorem sits on top: if the derivative exists at c, continuity there is guaranteed. The converse fails, as the V reminds us.

Practical takeaway: for a piecewise function only the junction points are doubtful; standard pieces are automatically smooth. And always test continuity first — if it fails, differentiability cannot hold, so you stop.
Here is the one proof from this subtopic that genuinely shows up in Boards, and the reasoning is elegant. We assume the derivative exists and squeeze out continuity.
We are given f dash c exists, a finite number. We want to show the limit of f of x minus f of c is zero, because that is exactly continuity restated.
The key algebraic trick: multiply and divide by x minus c. For x not equal to c this factor is non-zero, so we have changed absolutely nothing.
Why bother? Because the right side is now a product of two pieces we understand. The first is the difference quotient, the second is just x minus c.
Take the limit using the product rule for limits, valid because both limits exist and are finite. The first factor goes to f dash c, the second goes to zero, and the product is zero.
So the limit of f of x minus f of c is zero, which means the limit of f of x equals f of c. That is precisely continuity at c. Proof complete.

Notice we needed f dash c to exist for the first factor to have a finite limit. For the V at zero it does not exist, the argument collapses, and indeed the V is continuous without being differentiable. The arrow runs one way only.
A Board-favourite: we are handed a piecewise function and asked to choose the constant k that stitches the two pieces together continuously at the junction x equals two.
The first piece is two x plus three for x up to and including two, and the second is k x minus one beyond two. Only the junction is doubtful.
Step one, the value at the point. Since x equals two belongs to the first piece, f of two is two times two plus three, which is seven.
Step two, the left-hand limit. Approaching from below we still use the first piece, so the left-hand limit is also seven. So far, so consistent.
Step three, the right-hand limit. Approaching from above uses the second piece, giving two k minus one — and here the unknown k finally enters.
Step four, impose continuity: the right-hand limit must equal the value seven. So two k minus one equals seven, giving two k equals eight, hence k equals four.
So for k equal to four the two pieces meet at the common height seven, and the function is continuous at x equals two. That single equation did all the work.

board_events.text: LHD $= 4 \neq 3 =$ RHD $\Rightarrow$ not differentiable at $x = 2$, though continuous.
How many points is $f(x) = |x^{2}-4| + |x-1|$ non-differentiable?
A term $|g(x)|$ makes a corner exactly where $g(x)$ crosses zero AND changes sign.
The trap: $x = 0$ is the vertex of $x^{2}-4$, but the inside stays negative there — no sign change, no corner.
Adding functions smooths a kink only if both kink at the same place — here $-2, 1, 2$ are distinct.
Differentiable everywhere, yet $f'$ is not continuous at $0$
As $x \to 0$: the first term $\to 0$, but $\cos\frac{1}{x}$ oscillates forever — no limit.
$f'(0) = 0$ exists, yet $\lim_{x\to 0} f'(x)$ does not — $f'$ is discontinuous at $0$.
The four traps that cost marks here
Trap 1: believing continuous $\Rightarrow$ differentiable. It is the other way round.
Trap 2: skipping the continuity check before computing LHD and RHD.
Trap 3: miscounting modulus corners — count sign-changes of the inside, not zeros of its derivative.
Trap 4: over-counting endpoints in open intervals like $(0,3)$.
Mnemonic — DiCo, not CoDi: Differentiable $\Rightarrow$ Continuous, but Continuous does not $\Rightarrow$ Differentiable.

board_events.text: Why standard functions are continuous everywhere
If $f$ and $g$ are continuous at $c$, so are $f+g$, $f-g$, and $fg$.
The quotient $f/g$ is continuous at $c$ provided $g(c) \neq 0$.
The composite $f(g(x))$ is continuous if $g$ is continuous at $c$ and $f$ at $g(c)$.
So polynomials, $\sin x$, $\cos x$, $e^{x}$ and sensible combinations are continuous on their domains.
This is why only piecewise junctions ever need checking — the smooth interiors are guaranteed.

segments.text: There is a quieter idea hiding in the toolkit that explains a puzzle from the foundations: why we only ever checked junction points and trusted the smooth interiors.
The principle is this. If f and g are both continuous at a point, then their sum, their difference, and their product are all continuous there too. Continuity is preserved under these operations.
The quotient f over g is also continuous, but with one caveat: the denominator must be non-zero at the point. Divide by zero and continuity breaks, as one over x reminds us at the origin.
And composites are continuous too: if g is continuous at c and f is continuous at g of c, then f of g of x is continuous at c. Chaining continuous functions keeps you continuous.

This is exactly why polynomials, sine, cosine, e to the x, and all their sensible combinations are continuous wherever they are defined. They are built from continuous pieces by continuity-preserving operations.

And that closes the loop with the foundations: it is precisely why, for piecewise functions, only the suspicious junctions need checking. The smooth interiors are guaranteed continuous by this algebra.

One validity note to carry forward: the quotient rule needs the denominator non-zero, and each standard derivative holds only on its natural domain — log needs x positive, inverse secant needs magnitude of x above one.
Here is the spice rack itself — the standard derivatives you must recall instantly. Each holds on its natural domain. Let's walk the shelves.
The power rule: x to the n differentiates to n times x to the n minus one. And any constant differentiates to zero — flat lines have no slope.
The core trig trio: sine goes to cosine, cosine goes to minus sine — mind that negative — and tangent goes to secant squared.
The reciprocal trio: cotangent to minus cosecant squared, secant to secant tan, cosecant to minus cosecant cot. Notice cotangent and cosecant carry a minus sign.
The exponential and log shelf: e to the x is its own derivative, its party trick. A general a to the x picks up a natural-log-of-a factor, and natural log of x gives one over x.
Two headline inverse-trig results, which we will derive properly in a later part: inverse sine gives one over root one minus x squared, and inverse tan gives one over one plus x squared.
And a memory hook for the rest: the cofunctions — inverse cosine, inverse cotangent, inverse cosecant — have the same magnitude as their partners but carry a minus sign in front.
With the spice rack stocked, here are the combining techniques — the rules that let you differentiate sums, products, and quotients built from those ingredients.
The sum and difference rule is the friendly one: differentiate term by term. The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives — here the naive instinct is actually correct.
The constant-multiple rule: a constant just rides along outside. Differentiate the function and keep the constant sitting in front, untouched.
The product rule, our rectangle made rigorous: u dash v plus u v dash. Two terms, always. This is the one the naive guess gets wrong.
The quotient rule: low d-high minus high d-low, all over low squared. The order matters enormously — u dash v comes first, then minus u v dash, and the denominator is v squared.
Do not flip that numerator. It is u dash v minus u v dash, never the other way. Swapping the order silently negates your whole answer — the single most common quotient-rule sign error.

board_events.text: Spotting a product error, and a rationalising derivation
A student writes $\frac{d}{dx}(x^{2}\sin x) = 2x\cos x$. Why is that wrong?
The crime: applying the false rule $(uv)' = u'v'$ — multiplying the two derivatives.

board_events.text: Four toolkit traps, and one speed habit

Trap 3: trig-derivative sign slips — cos, cot, csc and their inverses all carry a minus.

Mnemonic: product = two strips; quotient = low d-high minus high d-low, over low-squared.
A function inside a function

segments.text: <curious>Two more: first the signature product-rule blunder, then a first-principles derivation that confirms the power rule for a fractional exponent.
A student differentiates x squared sine x and writes two x cosine x. This is the single most common differentiation error — can you see the crime before I say it?
The crime is applying the false rule: multiplying the two derivatives, two x and cosine x, into a single term. That forgets one whole strip of the rectangle.
The fix is the real product rule: two x sine x plus x squared cosine x, which factors as x times the bracket two sine x plus x cosine x. Two terms, exactly as promised.
Now first principles for one over root x. Combine the two fractions in the numerator over a common denominator; you get root x minus root x plus h on top.
Rationalise by multiplying top and bottom by root x plus root x plus h. The numerator becomes x minus x plus h, which is just minus h — and that h cancels the one downstairs.
Let h go to zero and the three root-x factors multiply to two x to the three halves, giving minus one over that. This is exactly the power rule on x to the minus one half. The rack checks out.
Let's bank the recurring toolkit mistakes and the habit that prevents most of them before they happen.
Trap one, the product trap again, because it never stops appearing. A product's derivative has two terms. A one-term answer to a product is wrong by inspection — no calculation needed.
Trap two, flipping the quotient order. It is u dash v minus u v dash over v squared, never the reverse. Anchor it with low d-high minus high d-low.
Trap three, trig sign slips. Cosine goes to minus sine — that negative is easy to drop. Group the negative ones mentally: cosine, cotangent, cosecant, and their three inverses.
Trap four, dropping domain restrictions. Natural log needs x positive; inverse secant carries an absolute value of x and lives only outside magnitude one. The domain is part of the answer.

The pro-tip that saves the most time: before grinding a quotient, check whether algebra simplifies it first. That sine over one plus cosine example collapsed a messy quotient rule into a one-line answer.
Carry two mnemonics out of here: a product is always two strips, and the quotient rhyme is low d-high minus high d-low, over low-squared. Those two lines cover most toolkit questions.
<curious>What happens when one operation is stacked on top of another? That is a composite function, and it needs its own rule to differentiate.
Take y equal to sine of x squared. That is two operations: first square the x, then take the sine of the result. You cannot reach for one single standard derivative here.

The cleanest picture is meshing gears. Turning x drives an intermediate shaft u, which drives the output y. If u spins three times per turn of x, and y spins five times per turn of u, then y spins fifteen times per turn of x.
Rates simply multiply along the chain. The rate of y with respect to x equals the rate of y with respect to u, times the rate of u with respect to x. Five times three is fifteen.
To use it, peel the function like an onion from the outside in. Differentiate the outer function while keeping the inner part untouched, then multiply by the derivative of the inner part.
For sine of x squared: the outer sine differentiates to cosine, evaluated at the untouched inner x squared. Then multiply by the inner derivative two x. The answer is two x cosine of x squared.
That final multiply-by-the-inside is the entire trick, and forgetting it is the number-one chain-rule error. Writing cosine of x squared and stopping is wrong — you still owe the extra factor two x.
Let's state the rule precisely, then the extended form for deeper nesting, then the patterns you will reuse constantly.

The two-link chain rule: if y is f of u and u is g of x, both differentiable, then the derivative is f dash evaluated at g of x, times g dash of x. Outer derivative at the inner, times inner derivative.
For three or more links, the chain just gets longer. For f of g of h of x, you peel three layers and pick up three factors, each layer contributing exactly one.
Now the workhorse patterns. A power of g: bring the exponent down, drop it by one, and multiply by g dash. This is the power rule with the chain factor attached.
Sine of g differentiates to cosine of g times g dash. And e to the g stays e to the g, but still owes the inner derivative g dash. The exponential's magic does not exempt it from the chain.
And natural log of g differentiates to g dash over g. Notice the same signature everywhere: the inner derivative g dash rides along as a multiplying factor. That factor is what students forget.

One validity note: both links must be differentiable — g at x, and f at g of x. If either link fails, at a corner or outside the domain, the rule does not apply there. Root u, for instance, breaks at u equals zero.
Two examples: a clean single-layer power, then a three-layer nest where you can literally count the factors as a completeness check.
First, y equal to three x squared plus five, all to the fourth power. The outer operation is to-the-fourth, the inner is three x squared plus five.
Bring the four down, drop the power to three, keep the inner intact, then multiply by the inner derivative six x. It tidies to twenty-four x times the bracket cubed.
Now a triple nest: sine of cosine of x squared. Three layers — outer sine, middle cosine, inner x squared. Peel from the outside in.
The outer sine gives cosine of cosine of x squared. The middle cosine gives minus sine of x squared. The inner x squared gives two x. Three factors, one per layer.
Tidy it up: minus two x, times sine of x squared, times cosine of cosine of x squared. Every layer you peeled contributed exactly one factor.
That is your completeness check for any nest: count the factors against the layers. Three layers must yield three factors. A missing factor means you dropped a layer somewhere.

First, y equal to three x squared plus five, all to the fourth power. The outer operation is to-the-fourth, the inner is three x squared plus five.

Tidy it up: minus two x, times sine of x squared, times cosine of cosine of x squared. Every layer you peeled contributed exactly one factor.
That is your completeness check for any nest: count the factors against the layers. Three layers must yield three factors. A missing factor means you dropped a layer somewhere.

A student writes $\frac{d}{dx}e^{3x} = e^{3x}$. What is missing?
Four chain traps, and a spoken habit
Trap 1: forgetting the inner derivative — every peeled layer owes a factor.
Trap 2: differentiating the inside too early — keep it intact inside the outer derivative.
Trap 3: losing a layer in deep nesting — count factors against layers.
Trap 4: mixing chain with product — apply the product rule first, chain on the composite factor.

Explicit versus implicit relations
The circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=25$ tangles $y$ with $x$ — solving for $y$ splits the curve messily.
The shift: even unwritten as a formula, $y$ is secretly a function of $x$ along the curve.

segments.text: First the most common chain slip in one line, then a harder example where the chain rule sits inside a product.
A student differentiates e to the three x and writes e to the three x, unchanged. They treated it like plain e to the x, which is its own derivative. What did they forget?
The inside is three x, whose derivative is three. So the real answer is e to the three x times three, that is three e to the three x. The forgot-to-multiply-by-the-inside error again.
<curious>Now the harder one: y equal to x squared times root one plus x squared. This combines the product rule with the chain rule — which do we apply first?

Set v as root one plus x squared, that is one plus x squared to the half. By the chain rule, v dash is one half times the bracket to the minus half, times two x, which simplifies to x over root one plus x squared.
Now the product rule with u as x squared and v as the root. u dash v gives two x root one plus x squared, and u v dash gives x squared times x over the root. Two terms.
Put over the common denominator root one plus x squared, combine the numerator to two x plus three x cubed, and factor out an x. The clean result is x times two plus three x squared, over the root.
Let's bank the chain-rule mistakes and the one out-loud habit that eliminates most of them.
Trap one, forgetting the inner derivative. Writing derivative of sine of two x as cosine of two x, without the times two. Every peeled layer owes a factor — no exceptions.
Trap two, differentiating the inside too early. Keep the inner function intact sitting inside the outer derivative; only its separate derivative becomes a multiplying factor afterwards.
Trap three, losing a layer in deep nesting. For a triple composite you need exactly three factors. Count them against your layers before you declare the answer done.
Trap four, tangling chain with product. When a composite sits inside a product, apply the product rule first, then use the chain rule to differentiate the composite factor. Order keeps it clean.

The pro-tip that beats every trap: say the recipe out loud. Derivative of the outside, times derivative of the inside. For each layer you strip, immediately append its factor before doing anything else.
Carry this line out of here: outside-in, and don't forget the inside. That mechanical rhythm alone kills the dropped-inner-factor error almost entirely.
<curious>So far y has always been served up neatly as y equals some expression in x. But many curves refuse to cooperate. What then?

Take the circle x squared plus y squared equals twenty-five. Here y is tangled up with x in one equation, not isolated. You could solve for y as plus or minus a root, but that is clumsy and splits the curve into two pieces.

The core idea is a small but powerful mental shift. Even though y is not written as a formula in x, it is secretly a function of x along the curve. So treat it as a hidden function and differentiate the whole equation.

Whenever you differentiate a term containing y, the chain rule kicks in and tacks on a dy dx. So the derivative of y squared is two y times dy dx, exactly as the derivative of box squared is two box times box dash.

For the circle, differentiate both sides: two x plus two y dy dx equals zero, which rearranges to dy dx equals minus x over y. The slope depends on both x and y — normal and fine for an implicit curve.
A pure x term differentiates normally; a y term always drags along its dy dx. Collect the dy dx terms and solve algebraically. That is the entire method in one line.

One caveat: where y equals zero, at the points plus and minus five comma zero, minus x over y blows up. The derivative does not exist there, and the formula is honestly reporting a vertical tangent — not an error.
Let's state the machinery cleanly: the governing principle, the mixed-term rule, and the step-by-step template you apply to any relation.

The governing principle: differentiate both sides with respect to x, applying the chain rule to every y term. A power of y gives n y to the n minus one, times dy dx. Any function of y gives f dash of y times dy dx.
Mixed x-y terms need the product rule too, since both factors depend on x. The derivative of x times y is one times y, plus x times dy dx — that is y plus x dy dx.
Now the general template for a relation. Step one, differentiate term by term: chain rule on the y terms, product rule on the mixed terms, ordinary differentiation on the pure x terms.
Step two, gather every dy dx term on one side of the equation and move everything else to the other side. You are setting up to factor.
Step three, factor out dy dx and divide to isolate it. The answer is generally an expression in both x and y — and that is expected, not a mistake.

For a second derivative, differentiate the first implicit derivative again with respect to x, then substitute the expression for dy dx back in, and use the original relation to simplify wherever you can.
Two examples: the circle as a warm-up, then the folium of Descartes, where a mixed x-y term forces the product rule.
First, find dy dx for x squared plus y squared equals a squared — a general circle of radius a. The a is just a constant here.
Differentiate both sides, chain rule on y squared: two x plus two y dy dx equals zero. The constant a squared differentiates to zero. Solve, and dy dx is minus x over y.
Now the folium of Descartes: x cubed plus y cubed equals three a x y. The right side has a mixed x y term, so watch for the product rule there.
Differentiate: chain rule on y cubed gives three y squared dy dx, and the product rule on x y gives y plus x dy dx. The whole right side carries the factor three a.
Divide through by three, then gather the dy dx terms on the left and the rest on the right. Factoring dy dx, its coefficient is y squared minus a x, and the right side is a y minus x squared.
Divide to isolate it: dy dx equals a y minus x squared, over y squared minus a x. Both x and y appear, exactly as expected for an implicit curve.

sections.title: The dropped-factor trap and a second derivative & related topics

board_events.text: Spotting the defining error, and going to $y''$
A student differentiates $x^{2}+y^{2}=1$ and writes $2x + 2y = 0$. What went wrong?
The tell: their equation has a $y$-term but no $\frac{dy}{dx}$ — they treated $y$ as a constant.
Four implicit traps, and the labelling habit
Trap 1: forgetting the $\frac{dy}{dx}$ on $y$-terms — $\frac{d}{dx}(y^{2}) = 2y\frac{dy}{dx}$, never just $2y$.
Trap 2: forgetting the product rule on mixed terms — $\frac{d}{dx}(xy) = y + x\frac{dy}{dx}$.
Trap 3: trying to pre-solve for $y$ — usually unnecessary and messy.
Trap 4: second-derivative shortcuts — you must substitute the first $\frac{dy}{dx}$ back in.

segments.text: First the defining sin of the topic caught in the act, then a second-derivative problem with a beautiful collapse at the end.
A student differentiates x squared plus y squared equals one and writes two x plus two y equals zero. Something is badly wrong — can you name it?
The tell is that their equation has a y term but no dy dx anywhere. They differentiated y squared as if y were a constant, getting two y instead of two y dy dx. Their line is not even a derivative.
The fix restores the chain factor: two x plus two y dy dx equals zero, giving dy dx equals minus x over y. Scan your work — a y term with no dy dx means a dropped chain factor.

Now the second derivative for the unit circle. We already have the first derivative, minus x over y. Differentiate it again with respect to x, using the quotient rule and remembering d by dx of y is dy dx.

The quotient rule gives minus, the bracket y minus x times dy dx, over y squared. Substitute dy dx as minus x over y, and the numerator becomes y plus x squared over y, which tidies to y squared plus x squared over y cubed.

<excited>Now the beautiful collapse: the original relation says x squared plus y squared is one, so the whole numerator becomes one, and the second derivative reduces to a clean minus one over y cubed.
Let's bank the implicit-differentiation mistakes and the one mental label that makes the whole topic automatic.
Trap one, the defining error: forgetting the dy dx on y terms. The derivative of y squared is two y dy dx, never just two y. Drop that factor and every answer downstream is corrupted.
Trap two, forgetting the product rule on mixed terms. The derivative of x y is y plus x dy dx, not dy dx alone. Both factors depend on x, so both strips must appear.
Trap three, trying to pre-solve for y before differentiating. That is usually unnecessary and messy. Differentiate the relation as it stands and let the algebra do the work.

Trap four, second-derivative shortcuts. When finding y double dash, you must substitute the first dy dx back in, and you may use the original relation to simplify. Skipping that leaves the answer half-done.
The master pro-tip: treat every y as if it wore a little bracket x label — y is y of x. Then implicit differentiation is just the chain rule, and the dy dx factors appear automatically.
The line to remember: it is just the chain rule in disguise — every y owes a dy dx. And final answers naturally involve both x and y; that is expected, not a mistake.
<curious>An inverse trig function answers a simple question: which angle gives this ratio? Inverse sine of x is the angle whose sine is x. Differentiating them needs no new magic.

If y is inverse sine of x, then sine y equals x. Differentiate both sides implicitly, which you just learned, and solve for dy dx. Out pops one over root one minus x squared. Every inverse-trig derivative is born this way.
But the real exam drama lies elsewhere. Examiners adore expressions like inverse tan of two x over one minus x squared, which look monstrous to differentiate head-on. The secret is to simplify first.
These are double-angle formulas in disguise. Let x equal tan theta. Then two x over one minus x squared becomes two tan theta over one minus tan squared theta, which is exactly tan of two theta.

The substitution triangle helps you see it: with x equals tan theta, the opposite side is x, the adjacent is one, and the hypotenuse is root one plus x squared. Every trig ratio of theta reads straight off this triangle.
So the monster equals inverse tan of tan two theta, which is two theta, which is two inverse tan of x. Differentiating that is a one-liner: two over one plus x squared. The brutal problem melts away.

<whisper>But read the fine print. The cancellation is only valid when two theta stays in the principal range of inverse tan. Outside it, the identity differs by a constant on each piece — so these simplifications are piecewise, and you must state the range.
Let's collect the six standard inverse-trig derivatives, then the golden substitution identities that unlock the hard problems.
Inverse sine gives one over root one minus x squared. Inverse cosine is the same magnitude with a minus sign. Both live on magnitude of x below one.
Inverse tan gives one over one plus x squared, valid for all real x. Inverse cotangent is again the same magnitude with a minus sign in front.
Inverse secant gives one over the absolute value of x, times root x squared minus one. Inverse cosecant carries the minus. That absolute value is essential, and both need magnitude of x above one.

Now the golden identities. Two inverse tan of x equals all three of these disguised forms: inverse tan of two x over one minus x squared, inverse sine of two x over one plus x squared, and inverse cosine of one minus x squared over one plus x squared.

Two more: two inverse sine of x equals inverse sine of two x root one minus x squared, and three inverse sine of x equals inverse sine of three x minus four x cubed. These are the double and triple angle sine formulas, read backwards.

And the substitution keys to memorise: the two x over one minus x squared and one minus x squared over one plus x squared forms scream x equals tan theta; two x root one minus x squared screams x equals sine theta; and root x squared minus one screams x equals secant theta.
Let's derive two of the standard results from implicit differentiation, then apply the plain chain rule to a simple inverse-tan.
Let y be inverse tan of x, so tan y equals x. Differentiate both sides: the chain rule on tan y gives secant squared y times dy dx, and that equals one.
So dy dx is one over secant squared y. Use the identity secant squared equals one plus tan squared, and tan y is x, so it becomes one over one plus x squared. Clean and derived, not memorised.
Similarly, let y be inverse sine of x, so sine y equals x. Differentiating gives cosine y times dy dx equals one, so dy dx is one over cosine y.
Write cosine y as root one minus sine squared y, taking the positive root because cosine is non-negative on the principal range. Since sine y is x, this is one over root one minus x squared.
Now a Board-level warm-up: differentiate inverse tan of two x. This is just the chain rule — outer derivative one over one plus the inside squared, times the inner derivative two.
The inside two x squares to four x squared, and the factor two rides on top, giving two over one plus four x squared. No substitution needed here — it is a genuine composite, not a disguise.

sections.title: Substitution power and the piecewise-sign trap & related topics

board_events.text: A monster that melts, and one that flips sign
For $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\lt x\le 1$: $y = \pi - 2\sin^{-1}x$, so $y' = -\frac{2}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$ — opposite sign!
Lesson: a single formula for all $x$ is wrong on half the domain — always check the principal range.
Half-angle magic on an intimidating fraction
The whole game: recognise the disguise, substitute, collapse, then differentiate the simple result.
Four inverse-trig traps, and a pattern-spotting eye
Trap 1: ignoring principal-range domains — the identities, and sometimes the derivative's sign, are piecewise.
Trap 2: table sign mix-ups — $\cos^{-1}, \cot^{-1}, \csc^{-1}$ carry the minus.
Trap 3: dropping $|x|$ in $\sec^{-1}$ and $\csc^{-1}$ — it matters for $x\lt -1$.
Trap 4: brute-forcing instead of substituting — grinding the quotient rule invites algebra errors.
Mnemonic: “Substitute, collapse the double angle, then differentiate — and mind the range.”
Three functions, one that breaks both rules
$x^{5}$: power rule (constant exponent). $5^{x}$: exponential rule (constant base).
$x^{x}$: variable base AND variable exponent — neither rule applies. We are stuck.
The log is a currency converter: it turns multiplication and powers into addition.
It also tames long products: $\ln$ shatters a product into a clean sum of logs.
Take the log, then differentiate — that single trick is logarithmic differentiation.
When $x$ and $y$ are both driven by a third variable
A cricket ball: time drives both height $y$ and horizontal distance $x$.
Time is the puppeteer; $x$ and $y$ are two puppets on its strings.
A Ferris wheel: your seat is $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$, driven by angle $\theta$.
Validity: the slope needs $dx/dt \neq 0$.
The differentiation just compares the puppets' motions — rates, then their ratio.

segments.text: Two substitution examples. The first melts cleanly. The second hides a trap so sharp it flips the sign of your derivative on half the domain.
First, differentiate inverse tan of two x over one minus x squared, on the interval minus one to one. Head-on this is painful, so substitute x equals tan theta.

The inside becomes tan of two theta. On this range two theta stays inside the principal interval, so the cancellation is valid: y is two theta, that is two inverse tan of x, and the derivative is two over one plus x squared.

Now the trap. Differentiate inverse sine of two x root one minus x squared. Substitute x equals sine theta, so two x root one minus x squared becomes two sine theta cosine theta, which is sine of two theta.
For magnitude of x up to one over root two, two theta stays in the principal range of inverse sine, so y is two inverse sine of x, and the derivative is two over root one minus x squared.

<whisper>But for x above one over root two, two theta leaves the principal range, and the identity becomes pi minus two inverse sine of x. Now the derivative is minus two over root one minus x squared — the opposite sign.

The lesson is sharp: a student who writes one formula for all x is wrong on half the domain. With inverse-trig substitutions, always check whether the multiple angle stays inside the principal range — the sign itself is piecewise.
<excited>An Advanced-level gem: an expression that looks genuinely intimidating collapses, through a half-angle identity, to a clean one half.

Differentiate inverse tan of the fraction root one plus x squared minus one, over x. Head-on this is a nightmare, so substitute x equals tan theta, which makes root one plus x squared equal secant theta.
The fraction becomes secant theta minus one over tan theta. Rewrite in sines and cosines, and it tidies to one minus cosine theta, over sine theta.

Now the half-angle identities: one minus cosine theta is two sine squared theta over two, and sine theta is two sine theta over two cosine theta over two. The twos and one sine cancel, leaving tan of theta over two.
So y is inverse tan of tan theta over two, which cancels to theta over two, which is one half inverse tan of x. The monster has become a clean multiple of a standard inverse tan.

Differentiating is now trivial: one half times one over one plus x squared, that is one over two times one plus x squared. A genuinely intimidating expression reduced to a clean half — the payoff of the substitution method.
That is the whole game of this subtopic: recognise the disguise, substitute the matching trig form, collapse the inner expression, and only then differentiate the simple result you are left with.
Let's bank the inverse-trig mistakes and the pattern recognition that turns a five-minute grind into a thirty-second answer.

Trap one, ignoring principal-range domains. Writing one simplified formula for all x. These identities, and sometimes even the sign of the derivative, are piecewise. Always check where the multiple angle stays in range.
Trap two, table sign mix-ups. The cofunctions — inverse cosine, inverse cotangent, inverse cosecant — carry minus signs. Pairing them wrongly with inverse sine, tan, or secant is a common slip.
Trap three, dropping the absolute value in inverse secant and inverse cosecant. That absolute value of x genuinely matters for x below minus one; without it your derivative has the wrong sign there.
Trap four, brute-forcing instead of substituting. Grinding the quotient or chain rule on two x over one minus x squared wastes time and invites algebra errors. Substitution is far safer and faster.
The pro-tip: train your eye to spot the disguises. Two x over one minus x squared screams tan theta; two x root one minus x squared screams sine theta; root x squared minus one screams secant theta.
The mnemonic to carry out: substitute, collapse the double angle, then differentiate — and mind the range. Recognising the pattern is the whole win here, but always finish by stating the valid range.
<curious>Differentiate three functions: x to the five, then five to the x, then x to the x. The first two are routine. The third breaks everything. Why?

x to the five is a piece of cake — the power rule handles a constant exponent, giving five x to the fourth. Five to the x is also routine — the exponential rule handles a constant base, giving five to the x times natural log of five.

But x to the x has a variable in both the base and the exponent at once. The power rule assumes the exponent stands still; the exponential rule assumes the base stands still. Here nothing stands still, so we are stuck.
This is where the logarithm rides in. Think of it as a currency converter in a busy market: it turns the hard currency of multiplication and powers into the easy currency of addition.
Take natural log of both sides of y equals x to the x. The troublesome exponent slides down to become an ordinary factor: log y equals x times log x, which we can actually differentiate.
It earns its keep a second way too: when y is a long, ugly product or quotient of many factors, log shatters that product into a clean sum of logs, and a sum is trivial to differentiate term by term.
That single trick — take the log, then differentiate — is logarithmic differentiation. One condition to remember: the base must be positive, since the log of a non-positive number is undefined.
Now the second idea. Sometimes x and y are not tied to each other directly; instead, both are controlled by a third, behind-the-scenes variable — a parameter, usually t for time or theta for angle.

Picture a cricket ball flying through the air. You do not naturally describe its height as a function of its horizontal distance. What you know is how time drives both — x from the horizontal speed, y from speed minus the pull of gravity.
Time is the puppeteer; x and y are the two puppets dangling from its strings. To get the slope of the ball's path, you ask how fast each puppet responds to the puppeteer and take the ratio.
So dy dx equals the rate of y with respect to t, divided by the rate of x with respect to t. Each is an ordinary derivative in the parameter; the ratio gives the slope in the x-y plane.
Or picture a giant wheel at a village fair: your seat's position is most naturally given by the rotation angle, x equals r cosine theta and y equals r sine theta. The angle is the puppet-master here.
One validity guard: the slope needs the rate of x with respect to t to be non-zero. Where that rate is zero, the slope blows up — a vertical tangent — and the formula breaks.

That is the whole intuition: with a parameter pulling the strings, differentiation just compares the puppets' motions — find each rate, then take their ratio. The second derivative, as we will see, needs one extra turn of the crank.

Four traps, and two direct-write shortcuts
Trap 1: dropping the $\frac{1}{y}$ — $\frac{d}{dx}\ln y = \frac{1}{y}\frac{dy}{dx}$, not $\frac{1}{y}$.
Trap 2: the half-rule on $u^{v}$ — writing only $u^{v}\ln u$ or only $v\,u^{v-1}$. You need their sum.
Trap 3: the parametric second-derivative ratio — always slope first, differentiate by $t$, divide by $dx/dt$.
Trap 4: ignoring the positive-base condition — use $|\cdot|$ or state the domain when the base can be $\le 0$.
For parametric curves, simplify $\frac{dy}{dx}$ fully before substituting a value — the constants almost always cancel.
The derivative of the derivative
For a moving car: first derivative = speed; second derivative = acceleration.

segments.text: Two parametric examples: the astroid, where everything cancels beautifully, then the second-derivative trap that examiners set again and again.
First the astroid, x equals a cosine cubed t and y equals a sine cubed t. Differentiate each with respect to t, using the chain rule on the cubes.
The rate of x is minus three a cosine squared t sine t, and the rate of y is three a sine squared t cosine t. Now take the ratio for the slope.

The three a's cancel, and one power each of sine and cosine cancels, leaving minus sine t over cosine t, that is minus tan t. That clean cancellation is the hallmark of a well-posed parametric problem.
Now the trap. For x equals a t squared and y equals two a t, the rate of y is two a and the rate of x is two a t, so the slope dy dx is one over t. So far, so easy.

<whisper>Here is the most-tested error: cancelling the d-t's and writing the second derivative as zero over two a, which is zero. That is simply wrong — it would falsely claim the parabola has zero curvature everywhere.

The correct route: differentiate the slope one over t with respect to t, giving minus one over t squared, then divide by the rate of x, two a t. The real answer is minus one over two a t cubed. Chant: slope, differentiate by t, divide by the rate of x.
<excited>An Advanced-level classic: given x equals sine t and y equals sine p t, prove a clean differential-equation relation. Watch the awkward terms annihilate at the end.
The target relation is one minus x squared times y double dash, minus x times y dash, plus p squared y, equals zero. We build up dy dx and y double dash parametrically.
The rate of x is cosine t, the rate of y is p cosine p t. So the first derivative, y dash, is p cosine p t over cosine t. Keep this handy.

For y double dash, differentiate that slope with respect to t by the quotient rule, then divide by cosine t once more. It comes out as minus p squared sine p t cosine t, plus p sine t cosine p t, all over cosine cubed t.

Now assemble, using one minus x squared equals one minus sine squared t equals cosine squared t. Multiplying y double dash by cosine squared t cancels two powers of cosine, leaving minus p squared sine p t, plus p sine t cosine p t over cosine t.
The middle term, x times y dash, is sine t times p cosine p t over cosine t, that is p sine t cosine p t over cosine t. And p squared y is simply p squared sine p t.

Add the three pieces. The two p sine t cosine p t over cosine t terms cancel each other, and the plus and minus p squared sine p t pair cancels too. Everything annihilates to zero — the relation holds identically. Proof done.
Let's bank the log and parametric mistakes, plus two shortcuts that let you write answers directly under time pressure.
Trap one, dropping the one over y. The derivative of log y is one over y times dy dx, not just one over y. The y is a function of x, so the chain rule demands that extra dy dx.

Trap two, the half-rule on u to the v. Writing only the exponential piece, or only the power piece. Both are halves of the truth; the real answer is their sum. A one-piece answer to u to the v is always incomplete.

Trap three, the parametric second-derivative ratio. Never use the ratio of the two second t-derivatives. Always: find the slope, differentiate it with respect to t, then divide by the rate of x once more.
Trap four, ignoring the positive-base condition. Log differentiation needs a positive base; if the base can be zero or negative, work with absolute values or restrict the domain, and say so.
The first pro-tip: for any u to the v, skip re-deriving and write the answer directly as the exponential piece plus the power piece. That single line covers every variable-power question.

The second pro-tip: for parametric curves, fully simplify dy dx before plugging in any value. The constants almost always cancel, and a clean symbolic slope is far less error-prone to substitute into.
<curious>The first derivative measures a rate of change. So what does the derivative of the derivative measure? Something you feel every time you accelerate.

For a moving car, the first derivative is the speedometer reading — how fast position changes. The second derivative measures how fast the rate itself is changing — that is the acceleration, how hard you press the pedal.
In symbols, the second derivative is the derivative of dy dx, written d two y by d x squared, or simply y double dash. You differentiate once, then differentiate the result again.

Geometrically, the second derivative tells you which way a curve bends. Where it is positive, the graph is concave up, a cup that could hold water. Where it is negative, it is concave down, a dome that sheds water.

So the first derivative tells you whether you are going uphill or downhill. The second tells you whether the road is curving toward the sky or toward the ground. They answer completely different questions.

For parametric curves, use the rule from the last subtopic — differentiate the slope by t, divide by the rate of x, never the naive ratio. For implicit relations, differentiate twice, chain-ruling every y term.
And one more reading: where the second derivative changes sign, the concavity flips — that point is an inflection point. The cube root example from the foundations flips exactly at the origin.
Now two Mean Value Theorems that sound abstract but describe something you live through constantly — a ball at its peak, and a speed camera on the expressway.
Start with Rolle. Throw a ball straight up and catch it at the same height it left your hand. At the very top of its flight, for one instant, it is neither rising nor falling — its velocity is zero.

Rolle makes this rigorous: if a smooth, unbroken function has equal values at two points, then somewhere strictly between them the slope must be zero. You went up and came back, so there had to be a flat moment at the turn.

Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem is the grown-up generalization. Drive one hundred fifty kilometres in two hours; your average speed was seventy-five. MVT guarantees that at some instant your speedometer read exactly seventy-five.

In symbols, there is a point c where the instantaneous slope equals the average slope across the interval. Geometrically, some tangent is parallel to the secant joining the endpoints. This is exactly how average-speed cameras catch you.

The picture says it all: the green secant joins the endpoints, and somewhere inside, the dashed tangent at c runs exactly parallel to it. Rolle is just the special case where that secant happens to be horizontal.

Both theorems demand continuity on the closed interval and differentiability on the open interval, with Rolle adding equal endpoints. Drop even one and the guarantee collapses — the V on minus one to one has equal heights yet no flat spot, because it is not differentiable at its corner.

board_events.text: The precise statements to quote in exams

board_events.latex: \text{Parametric: } y'' = \frac{\frac{d}{dt}(dy/dx)}{dx/dt}; \quad \text{Implicit: differentiate twice, each } y \text{ carries } \tfrac{dy}{dx}
\text{Rolle: } f \text{ cont. on } [a,b],\; \text{diff. on } (a,b),\; f(a)=f(b) \Rightarrow \exists\, c: f'(c)=0
\text{Lagrange: } f \text{ cont. on } [a,b],\; \text{diff. on } (a,b) \Rightarrow \exists\, c: f'(c) = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}

The derivative is $-1$ on the left, $+1$ on the right — never zero. Panic?
The resolution: differentiability fails at the corner $x = 1 \in (0,2)$, so Rolle does not apply — the conclusion is not promised.

Four traps, and two default weapons
Trap 1: applying a theorem without checking hypotheses — the $|x|$ / step-function / piecewise trap.
Trap 2: confusing Rolle with MVT — Rolle needs $f(a)=f(b)$ and concludes $f'(c)=0$.
Trap 3: accepting a $c$ outside the open interval — it must lie strictly inside $(a,b)$.
Trap 4: the parametric/implicit second-derivative slip again — never the naive ratio.

segments.text: Let's pin down the exact statements you quote in an answer: the second-derivative forms, then Rolle and Lagrange with their hypotheses spelled out.
The second derivative is the derivative of the first derivative, and its sign gives concavity: positive is a cup, negative is a cap. That is the direct case for an explicit function of x.

Two carried-over forms: for parametric, differentiate the slope by t and divide by the rate of x, never the naive ratio. For implicit, differentiate the relation twice, remembering each y term carries a dy dx factor.

Rolle's theorem: if f is continuous on the closed interval, differentiable on the open interval, and takes equal values at the endpoints, then there exists at least one c inside where the derivative is zero.

Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem: with the same continuity and differentiability, but no equal-endpoints requirement, there exists at least one c inside where the instantaneous slope equals the average slope.
Read the fine print: both are existence theorems. They guarantee at least one such c exists, but say nothing about whether it is unique, and you still have to solve for it yourself.

The validity conditions are the hypotheses themselves: always confirm continuity on the closed interval and differentiability on the open interval, plus equal endpoints for Rolle, before using either conclusion. Any corner, cusp, or break inside voids the theorem.
First the cleanest proof in the subtopic — deriving MVT from Rolle — then a Board-favourite second-order relation to prove.

Rolle only fires when the endpoints are level, so we tilt the function to make them level. Define an auxiliary g of x as f minus the straight secant line joining the two endpoints. So g measures the vertical gap between the curve and the secant.

At the endpoints the curve meets the secant, so the gap is zero at both. g is continuous and differentiable because it is f minus a polynomial. We have manufactured exactly the equal-endpoints condition Rolle needs.
Apply Rolle to g: there exists a c inside the interval where g dash of c is zero. That single application is the whole engine of the proof.

Differentiate g: g dash is f dash minus the constant average slope. Setting g dash of c to zero gives f dash of c equals the average slope. That is Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem, proved. Subtracting the secant was the whole trick.
Now the relation. For y equals e to the x sine x, the product rule gives y dash equals e to the x sine x plus e to the x cosine x, which factors as e to the x times sine x plus cosine x.

Differentiate again: y double dash comes out as two e to the x cosine x. Substitute into y double dash minus two y dash plus two y, and every term cancels in pairs, leaving zero. The relation holds. Proof complete.
Two examples: verifying Rolle cleanly for sine, then the classic trap where the obvious condition holds but a hidden hypothesis quietly fails.
Verify Rolle for sine x on the interval zero to pi, and find the point c. First we check all three hypotheses hold.
Sine is continuous and differentiable everywhere, so certainly on this interval. The endpoints: sine of zero is zero, and sine of pi is also zero, so the values are equal. All three conditions hold.

Now find c: set f dash of c, which is cosine c, equal to zero. That gives c equals pi over two, which lies strictly inside the interval. Rolle is verified — the tangent at the peak of the sine curve is horizontal.

<curious>Now the trap. Apply Rolle to the absolute value of x minus one on zero to two. The endpoints look perfect: f of zero is one, f of two is one, so the equal-endpoints condition holds. A student charges ahead…
…tries to solve f dash of c equals zero, finds the derivative is minus one on the left and plus one on the right, never zero, and panics, assuming an arithmetic error. But there is no error.

The resolution: Rolle simply does not apply. The differentiability hypothesis fails at the corner x equals one, inside the interval. With a hypothesis violated, the conclusion is not promised — and indeed it fails. Always validate continuity and differentiability before reaching for the conclusion.
<excited>The signature power of MVT: choose the right function, and an apparently unprovable inequality falls out in just three lines.
The target: for zero less than a less than b, show that b minus a over b is less than log of b over a, which is less than b minus a over a. Two inequalities to pin at once.
The move is to apply the Mean Value Theorem to f of x equals log x on the interval a to b. Log x is continuous and differentiable for positive x, so the hypotheses hold.
MVT gives a c between a and b where f dash of c equals the average slope. Since the derivative of log is one over x, this reads one over c equals log of b over a, over b minus a.

Now the key step. Because c lies strictly between a and b, all positive, reciprocating reverses the order: one over b is less than one over c, which is less than one over a. Reciprocals flip inequalities for positive numbers.
Substitute one over c as log of b over a, over b minus a, into the middle. Now the sandwich reads one over b, less than log of b over a over b minus a, less than one over a.

Finish by multiplying throughout by b minus a, which is positive, so the inequalities are preserved. Out drops exactly the target: b minus a over b, less than log b over a, less than b minus a over a. Choose the right function and the bounds on c read straight off.
Let's bank the second-order and Mean-Value mistakes, and the two default strategies for the hardest questions.

Trap one, applying a theorem without checking hypotheses. The classic absolute-value, greatest-integer, or piecewise trap satisfies the obvious condition while quietly breaking continuity or differentiability. Always validate both first.

Trap two, confusing Rolle with MVT. Rolle additionally needs equal endpoints and concludes the slope is zero; MVT needs no such equality and concludes the slope equals the average. Using slope equals zero when the endpoints differ is wrong.
Trap three, accepting a c outside the open interval. The guaranteed point must lie strictly inside a to b. A solution landing on an endpoint does not count toward verifying the theorem.

Trap four, the same second-derivative slip from the parametric subtopic. Never write y double dash as the ratio of the two second t-derivatives. Differentiate the slope by t, then divide by the rate of x again.

The first pro-tip, for JEE Advanced: MVT is the default weapon for inequality proofs. Choose f so that f dash of c is exactly the quantity you want to bound, then squeeze using a less than c less than b.

The second pro-tip: for how-many-roots questions, reach for Rolle — two roots always manufacture a zero of the derivative between them. And remember, Rolle is just MVT with a horizontal secant: learn one picture, get both.

The engine of log differentiation: the derivative of log y is one over y, times dy dx. Never forget that one-over-y — it is the chain rule on log y, and dropping it silently corrupts every answer.

The master formula for u to the v: it is the sum of two pieces. The exponential-rule piece, with the base frozen, is u to the v times log u times v dash. The power-rule piece, with the exponent frozen, is v times u to the v minus one times u dash.
The log properties you use to simplify before differentiating: log of a product is a sum of logs, log of a quotient is a difference, and log of a power brings the exponent down to the front.
The parametric first derivative: with x and y both functions of t, dy dx is the rate of y over the rate of x, both taken in t. Valid wherever the rate of x is non-zero.
The parametric second derivative: differentiate the already-found slope with respect to t, then divide by the rate of x once more. This comes from applying the chain-rule operator a second time.

And the sharp warning: the second derivative is not the ratio of the two second t-derivatives. You cannot cancel the d-t's like numbers. Slope first, differentiate by t, divide by the rate of x one more time.
Let's derive the master formula so you trust it, then apply logarithmic differentiation to the classic x to the sine x.
Start with y equals f of x to the g of x, with f positive so the log is defined. Take the natural log of both sides; the exponent g slides down to the front, giving log y equals g times log f.
Differentiate both sides. The left uses the chain rule on log y, giving one over y times dy dx. The right uses the product rule on g times log f, giving g dash log f plus g times f dash over f.

parametric first derivative: x aur y dono t ke functions hone par, dy dx hai rate of y over rate of x, dono t mein liye hue. jahan rate of x non-zero hai, wahan valid.
parametric second derivative: pehle se mili slope ko t ke respect mein differentiate karo, phir rate of x se ek baar aur divide karo. yah chain-rule operator ko doosri baar lagane se aata hai.

aur teekhi warning: second derivative, do second t-derivatives ka ratio nahin hai. aap d-t ko numbers ki tarah cancel nahin kar sakte. pehle slope, fir t se differentiate, fir rate of x se ek baar aur divide.
chaliye master formula derive karte hain taaki aap bharosa karo, phir classic x to the sine x par logarithmic differentiation lagate hain.
y equals f of x to the g of x se shuru karo, f positive taaki log defined ho. Dono sides ka natural log lo; exponent g aage neeche khisakta hai, deta hai log y equals g times log f.

donon sides differentiate karo. left, log y par chain rule use karta hai, deta hai one over y times dy dx. right, g times log f par product rule use karta hai, deta hai g dash log f plus g times f dash over f.
y se multiply karo aur y ko f to the g wapas substitute karo. yahi master formula hai: poora original function, times wo bracket jo exponential piece aur power piece ko jodta hai.
ab application. y equals x to the sine x ke liye, logs lo: log y equals sine x times log x. exponent aur base dono variable hain, to ise sach mein log trick chahiye.
Differentiate karo: left deta hai one over y times dy dx. right, product rule se, deta hai cosine x times log x, plus sine x times one over x.

y se multiply karo aur wapas substitute karo: derivative hai x to the sine x, times bracket cosine x log x plus sine x over x. dhyan do master formula aur take-logs method kaise perfectly agree karte hain.

ek point par continuity: left-hand limit equals right-hand limit equals value. Differentiability: do one-sided derivatives equal aur finite. aur bridge — differentiable implies continuous, sirf ek taraf.
Toolkit basics: power rule, trig derivatives, product rule apne do terms ke saath, aur quotient rule — low d-high minus high d-low, over low squared.
Chain rule: rates chain ke saath multiply hoti hain. Iske patterns — sine of g, e to the g, log of g — har ek inner derivative g dash ko factor ki tarah rakhta hai. Wo factor kabhi mat bhoolo.
Implicit differentiation: har y term ek dy dx rakhta hai, aur mixed x-y terms product rule use karte hain. Phir dy dx terms ikattha karke solve karo; answer x aur y dono rakhta hai.

Inverse trig: inverse sine deta hai one over root one minus x squared, inverse tan deta hai one over one plus x squared, cofunctions minus rakhte hain. aur golden identity, two inverse tan of x equals inverse tan of two x over one minus x squared — range ka dhyan.

Logarithmic aur parametric: u to the v hai exponential piece plus power piece. parametric slope, t-rates ka ratio hai; parametric second derivative hai slope ko t se differentiate, over rate of x — kabhi naive ratio nahi.

aur Mean Value Theorems: Rolle, equal endpoints ke saath, andar ek zero slope guarantee karta hai. Lagrange ek interior slope guarantee karta hai jo average slope ke barabar hai. Rolle bas horizontal secant wala MVT hai.
